note: Track styles, step 4: the changes of a jazz standard, a major ii–V–I chained to the ii–V–i of the relative minor, heard over a swing backing track; then the turnaround named by number; then the chain again without looking. The two homes are ringed on a staff and named the long way, every chord is a chord token, and the key is moves with a {{?key}} line on what stays the same.

exercise.title: Jazz standards: ii–V–Is in a chain
exercise.why: A jazz standard is mostly ii–V–Is joined end to end, in the major key and in its relative minor, so spotting a ii–V tells you which home chord comes next.

cells.text: {{chord:Imaj7}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}, and {{chord:vi7}} is the 6th chord, built on {{6}}: the home chord of the relative minor. Tap the two ringed notes on the staff below to hear the two homes.

Press Play below to start the backing track. Bars 1 to 3 are a ii–V–I in {{=key}} major: {{chord:ii7}} is the 2nd chord and {{chord:V7}} the 5th, leading to {{chord:Imaj7}}. Bar 4 is {{chord:IVmaj7}}, the 4th chord. Bars 5 to 7 are a ii–V–i in the relative minor: {{chord:vii°7}} and {{chord:III7}}, leading to {{chord:vi7}}.
Call out "major" or "minor" each time the backing track lands on a home chord.
Practice until you hear each landing coming a bar early.

Press Play below to start the backing track: four chords that end a chorus and lead back to its top, {{chord:Imaj7}}, {{chord:vi7}}, {{chord:ii7}} and {{chord:V7}}. The last two are a ii and a V, so they point back to {{chord:Imaj7}} at the top of the next round. Say the number of each chord as it arrives: 1, 6, 2 or 5.
Practice until the numbers come without looking at the chord boxes.

Press Play below to start the backing track: the eight bars of the chain again. Look away from the chord boxes and call out "major" or "minor" on each home chord, then look back to check.
{{?key}}In another key the chords have other names, and the chain is the same: a ii–V–I in major, then a ii–V–i in its relative minor.
